questions.prompt: Order these from the LEAST architectural investment deserved to the MOST (proportionate architecture).

items.text: A simple internal CRUD admin screen with no rules
A long-lived pricing engine with complex, changing rules

questions.explanation: Match investment to stakes: a throwaway spike needs almost none, simple CRUD needs little, and a complex long-lived engine justifies the full Clean Architecture stack.

questions.prompt: When might a SIMPLER design (not full Clean Architecture) be the right call? Select all that apply.

options.text: Short-lived or throwaway code (a script or spike)
Simple CRUD with little business logic
A tiny app that fits in your head and won't grow
A large, long-lived system with complex, changing rules

questions.explanation: Simpler is often better for throwaway, trivial-CRUD, or tiny apps. A large, long-lived system with complex rules is exactly where full Clean Architecture pays off.

questions.prompt: The failure mode of TOO LITTLE structure — a haphazard, sprawling system with no discernible architecture — is called a Big Ball of ______.
questions.explanation: Foote & Yoder's 'Big Ball of Mud' is the risk of no architecture. The answer isn't 'no architecture' but proportionate architecture.

questions.prompt: What is the real goal that all of Clean Architecture's rules serve?

options.text: Adding as many layers as possible
Minimizing the cost of change and keeping options open

questions.explanation: The measure is always the cost of change and keeping options open — not conformance to a diagram or a layer count. Abstractions that don't lower change cost should be removed.

questions.prompt: Match each anti-pattern to its description.

pairs.right: Interfaces/layers with no real need — a YAGNI violation
Passing entities or ORM rows across boundaries, recoupling layers
A use case that only forwards to a gateway, adding a pointless boundary
Following the rules as laws instead of serving the cost-of-change goal

questions.explanation: These are the common ways Clean Architecture is misapplied; each trades real cost for no benefit.

questions.prompt: Should Clean Architecture's rules be treated as strict, unbreakable laws?

options.text: Yes — always add a port, never skip a layer
No — they're heuristics serving the cost-of-change goal; architects decide which boundaries to implement and which to ignore
Yes — the diagram is the law
No — you should ignore them entirely

questions.explanation: The rules are heuristics. Where a rule stops serving cheap change in a given spot, it's the wrong rule there — but the answer is proportionate architecture, not none.
